Detention Without Physical Examination of All Dried Shark Fins, Dried Fish Maws and Dried Shark Cartilage Powder Due to Filth
Detention Without Physical Examination of Seafood Products That Appear To Be Misbranded
why: General seafood misbranding alert; broader than shrimp but the only India-relevant seafood export line in the 15 categories.

t: Detention Without Physical Examination of Fish and Fishery Products Due to Decomposition and/or Histamine, and/or Indole
why: Decomposition/histamine is a seafood-handling (cold-chain) issue distinct from the nitrofurans/antibiotics story already in the Phase 3 sheet — a second, real seafood risk vector worth knowing about even though it did not show up as a dominant Phase 1 US charge code for shrimp.

t: Detention Without Physical Examination of Fish and Fishery Products for Importer and Foreign Processor (Manufacturer) Combinations
why: Firm-specific listing mechanism — relevant to understanding how an individual Indian shrimp processor gets targeted, not a hazard in itself.

t: Detention Without Physical Examination of Fish and Fishery Products From Foreign Processors Not in Compliance With Seafood HACCP Regulation
why: Process-control (HACCP) compliance, not a residue/contamination limit — a GMP-type finding, same category as the "filth" qualitative standard discussed elsewhere in Phase 3.

t: Detention Without Physical Examination of Aquaculture Seafood Products Due to Unapproved Drugs
why: Sibling alert to 16-129 (nitrofurans) — covers OTHER unapproved veterinary drugs in farmed shrimp beyond nitrofurans specifically (e.g. chloramphenicol, malachite green). Should be read alongside the Phase 3 shrimp row.

t: Detention Without Physical Examination of Seafood Products Due to Nitrofurans
why: Already cited directly in the Phase 3 sheet's shrimp row — the single most consequential shrimp-specific alert, with multiple named Indian firms on the current Red List.

t: Detention Without Physical Examination of Fresh and Fresh Frozen Lobster/Lobster Tails From India
Detention Without Physical Examination of Raw and Cooked Shrimp From India
why: A broader, India-specific shrimp alert (not limited to the nitrofurans hazard) — worth citing alongside 16-129 since it shows shrimp from India carries multiple, independent DWPE mechanisms, not just the antibiotic-residue one.

t: Detention Without Physical Examination of Seafood Products Due to the Presence of Salmonella
why: Salmonella in seafood specifically — relevant since Salmonella is also the dominant FDA charge code for several spice categories (see 99-19 below), showing it as a cross-cutting hazard rather than one confined to any single product.

t: Detention Without Physical Examination of Tamarind and Tamarind Products Due to Filth
Detention Without Physical Examination of Coconut Due to Microbiological Contamination
Detention Without Physical Examination of Food Products Due to the Presence of Mycotoxins
why: Directly names the same mycotoxin (aflatoxin, DON, fumonisin, ochratoxin A) hazard already quantified in the Phase 3 sheet for groundnuts and chilli; India appears extensively on this alert's Red List across multiple product types.

t: Detention Without Physical Examination of Black Pepper From India
why: India's only single-commodity, single-country FDA import alert among the 15 categories — in force since 1987 for filth/Salmonella; cited directly in the Phase 3 black-pepper row.

t: Detention Without Physical Examination of Honey and Blended Syrup Due to Unsafe Drug Residues
Detention Without Physical Examination of Adulterated and Misbranded Infant Formula
Detention Without Physical Examination and Guidance of Foods Containing Illegal and/or Undeclared Colors
why: Directly relevant to the Rhodamine B / methyl yellow illegal-colorant finding flagged in the Phase 3 turmeric row — this is the actual mechanism FDA uses to act on that hazard.

t: Detention Without Physical Examination of Cosmetics Due to Color Additive Violations
Detention Without Physical Examination of Cosmetics Due to Microbiological Contamination
Detention Without Physical Examination of Dietary Supplement Products From Firms That Have Not Met Dietary Supplement GMP
why: GMP-compliance mechanism directly relevant to herbal/botanical supplement exporters — a facility-level, not a formula-level, requirement, so it is fixable by process certification rather than product reformulation.

t: Detention Without Physical Examination of Products Marketed as Foods, Including Dietary Supplements, That Contain an Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient
why: Directly the same "unapproved drug / unauthorized health claim" hazard already in the Phase 3 herbal-supplements row — this alert is the enforcement mechanism, and its presence confirms the hazard is being formally tracked at the firm level, not just charge-coded case by case.

Detention Without Physical Examination of Raw Agricultural Products for Pesticides
why: The general-purpose pesticide-residue DWPE mechanism — this (plus 99-08 below) is the actual enforcement vehicle behind essentially every "pesticide residues" / "chemical contamination" FDA charge code already counted across the Phase 1 dataset and the chlorpyrifos findings in Phase 3.

t: Detention Without Physical Examination of Processed Human and Animal Foods for Pesticides
why: Sibling to 99-05 for processed/powdered forms — together these two alerts are the single most consequential pair on this whole list for the Phase 1/3 pesticide-residue findings (chlorpyrifos, tricyclazole, ethylene oxide).

t: Detention Without Physical Examination of Food Products Due to the Presence of Salmonella
why: The general Salmonella DWPE mechanism for food products generally (explicitly excludes black pepper, which has its own dedicated alert 28-02, and seafood, which has 16-81) — directly the enforcement vehicle behind the Salmonella/microbiological-contamination charge codes that dominate several spice categories' FDA refusal counts in this dataset.

t: Detention Without Physical Examination of Food Products Containing Undeclared Added Sulfiting Agents
Detention Without Physical Examination of Foods Containing Undeclared Major Food Allergens
why: Directly matches the one "undeclared allergen mustard in ground coriander" finding surfaced in the coriander RASFF records — a labeling/cross-contamination issue, not a residue-limit one.

Detention Without Physical Examination of Low-Acid Canned Foods Due to Inadequate Process Control
Detention Without Physical Examination of Imported Food Products That Appear to Be Misbranded
why: General misbranding DWPE mechanism — matches the "labeling/misbranding" FDA charge-code bucket already present in several categories' Phase 1 counts.

t: Detention Without Physical Examination of Foods Due to Heavy Metal (Toxic Element) Contamination
why: Directly matches the "chemical/heavy-metal contamination" FDA charge-code bucket that is a top-2 reason for Fenugreek specifically in the Phase 1 US data (5 of 16 rows) — this alert is likely the enforcement vehicle, though the specific metal (lead is common in turmeric/spice adulteration cases generally) is not named in FDA's public bulk refusal data per this project's existing epistemic-honesty note.

t: Detention Without Physical Examination of Ready-To-Eat Foods Prepared/Packed/Held Under Insanitary Conditions
why: The general insanitary-conditions (GMP) DWPE mechanism — this is the enforcement vehicle behind the "filth / insanitary conditions" charge-code bucket that is a top reason across almost every spice category in the Phase 1 US data, reinforcing that this is a facility/process finding, not a residue-limit one.

t: Detention Without Physical Examination of Food Products That Are or Contain an Unsafe Food Additive
why: Matches the "unauthorized additive/colorant" FDA charge-code bucket that is fennel's single dominant US refusal reason (28 of 39 rows) and part of turmeric's illegal-colorant finding.

t: Detention Without Physical Examination of Imported Human Foods Due to Filth
why: General filth DWPE mechanism, sibling to 99-43 (insanitary conditions) — together these cover the qualitative, non-MRL "filth/GMP" hazard type discussed throughout the Phase 3 sheet.

t: Detention Without Physical Examination of Human Food Products That Appear to Be Adulterated for Economic Gain
why: Economic-adulteration DWPE mechanism — directly relevant to the Rhodamine B/methyl yellow illegal-dye finding in turmeric, since colouring turmeric to mask lower quality or bulk it up is textbook economic adulteration.
